extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers working on worldbuilding and speculative/genre fiction (TV writers, novelists, short story authors)
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for fiction writers on how far to push weirdness in worldbuilding and how to introduce/pace strange elements so readers remain engaged. Covers TV, short fiction, and novels with examples and practical heuristics.

rubrics_metrics.name: One bye
rubrics_metrics.description: You get one bye: early on you ask the audience to believe one big thing; everything else has to follow from that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a pilot's premise (giant alien monoliths erupting) can be the single premise the audience accepts; you shouldn't also introduce unrelated huge shifts (e.g., armies of flying elephants) unless they are derived from that bye. Use the one-bye to anchor all subsequent weirdness so the world feels coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Oh, it's magic' anti-pattern / No magic as catch-all
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of 'Oh, it's magic' so anything goes — you don't get to throw things in without rules or consequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If magic (or an equivalent) is your bye, define its scope or show how other elements derive from it; avoid using 'magic' as a lazy explanation for arbitrary events because that undermines coherence and reader buy-in.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect genre and audience expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: How weird you can get depends on the expectations of your audience and the genre you are writing in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Urban fantasy, new weird, comic SF, and epic fantasy each carry different allowances for strange elements (e.g., urban fantasy accepts an encroaching magical force; new weird may allow broad strangeness but often keeps some physical laws intact). Signal genre expectations early so readers know what to expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make sure the audience knows where they are and what they are doing (clarity of orientation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set up the world so the audience understands their footing — where they are and what they're doing — otherwise they may be lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In pilots and openings especially, orient the audience quickly; lack of orientation can make even excellent worldbuilding feel inaccessible on first read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connect additional weirdness to the initial premise (internal consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can do more weird things if you connect them to the first bye; new strange elements should flow from the core premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: subsequent phenomena should be explained as consequences or extensions of the monoliths/initial weird element rather than unrelated surprises. This preserves cohesion and reduces perceived arbitrariness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weirdness budget (manage reader's cognitive/attentional budget)
rubrics_metrics.description: Weirdness, boredom, and other challenges all draw on a reader's 'budget' — too much expenditure and you lose them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Think of introducing oddness, long exposition, deep emotional beats, and pacing as competing uses of reader attention. Prioritize and limit what you ask readers to process at once; excessive weirdness or long stretches of boredom both risk losing engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce weirdness slowly — learning curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Add weirdness incrementally, building off previously established weirdness so readers have a learning curve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slowly layering new elements helps them feel normal by the time they accumulate; sudden, dense introductions of many strange things can overwhelm readers (though re-reading may later make such density rewarding).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use narrative voice as the familiar anchor
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong familiar voice can 'sell' or normalize extreme weirdness to readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Hitchhiker's Guide uses a narrative voice and an in-world guidebook to frame bizarre events as part of the joke, making the absurd acceptable. If voice remains a relatable touchstone, it can justify more radical departures in worldbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep characters relatable to ground worldbuilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Relatable characters provide a familiar center; if characters remain recognizable, the world can be weirder without losing readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when characters are themselves strange, ground readers with human emotions, motivations, or perspectives so they have something to anchor to amid exotic details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short fiction economy — expect only one bye
rubrics_metrics.description: In short fiction you generally get one bye because every weirdness costs words to explain; short stories typically explore a single idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allocate limited word-count to the core strange element and its consequences rather than multiple unrelated oddities; be precise about what you need the reader to accept and spend exposition carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Worldbuilding depth vs breadth — dig deep into one concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer depth (digging into one concept) over breadth (many shallow weird things) to create satisfying worldbuilding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing a single premise in detail yields more believable and engaging worlds than scattering many unexplored oddities that feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid arbitrary shifts in core world elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't change or remove multiple fundamental aspects of reality or society without justification — too many core shifts feel arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: altering major institutions (e.g., 'the Vatican doesn't exist') or fundamental rules without grounding will fragment reader trust. Limit large-scale alterations or ensure they are motivated within the world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pace weird revelations — one odd thing at a time
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce strange elements one at a time rather than piling them on simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The tactic of revealing oddness sequentially lets readers incorporate each new detail; this pacing preserves comprehension and reduces cognitive overload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use beta readers / early feedback to calibrate weirdness
rubrics_metrics.description: Rely on beta readers and early looks to gauge whether your world is too weird or confusing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test audiences can tell you where they felt lost, bored, or overloaded; use that feedback to adjust pacing, exposition, and the number of departures from the familiar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being 'too boring for too long' (engagement rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: The only firm rule of screenwriting quoted here: you can't be too boring for too long.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim or restructure exposition and scenes that slow momentum excessively. Boredom is itself a challenge that depletes reader/viewer budget and can make even interesting weirdness feel inaccessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that some works require re-reading (target audience awareness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors intentionally frontload opacity (Iain Banks example) and expect readers to re-read; this can be acceptable for a particular target audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you intend your work to reward re-reading, be aware that it narrows the initial audience; decide whether you want immediate accessibility or a design that assumes repeated reading and a specific readership.
